content: Nocturnal asthma is characterized by a reduction in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) of at least 15% between bedtime and awakening in individuals who exhibit both clinical and physiological evidence of asthma. The underlying pathophysiology of nocturnal asthma is intricately linked to chronobiology, which is the study of biological processes that follow time-related rhythms. Therefore, understanding the circadian rhythm is crucial for interpreting the changes in pulmonary function that occur in asthmatic patients during sleep. A population-based survey involving 7,729 patients revealed that approximately 74% of individuals with asthma reported waking up at least once per week due to symptoms. Furthermore, 64% of these patients experienced nocturnal awakenings with symptoms three times per week, and 39% reported waking up every night because of asthma-related symptoms. Nocturnal exacerbation of asthma is a highly prevalent clinical phenomenon, affecting roughly 75% of asthmatic individuals who wake up at least once per week due to symptoms. Additionally, approximately 40% of asthmatic patients experience nocturnal symptoms on a nightly basis.
